text:
Individual patient data meta-analysis by Simonis, Serpa Neto, Gama de Abreu, Pelosi and Schultz (Critical Care 2015) examining whether tidal volume size during mechanical ventilation is associated with pulmonary complications in ICU patients who do NOT have ARDS at the start of ventilation.

METHODS: The authors pooled individual patient data from 7 investigations covering 2,184 critically ill ICU patients ventilated without ARDS. Patients were grouped by tidal volume: 7 ml/kg of predicted body weight (PBW) or less; 7 to 10 ml/kg PBW; or 10 ml/kg PBW or more. The primary outcome was pulmonary complications, defined as a composite of developing ARDS or pneumonia during the hospital stay. Secondary outcomes included ICU and hospital length of stay and in-hospital mortality.

RESULTS: Pulmonary complications occurred in 23% of patients ventilated at 7 ml/kg PBW or less, 28% in the 7 to 10 ml/kg PBW group, and 31% in the group ventilated at 10 ml/kg PBW or more. After adjustment, ventilation with the lowest tidal volumes was associated with fewer pulmonary complications (adjusted risk ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.52 to 0.98; P = 0.042). Patients who developed pulmonary complications had fewer ICU-free days and hospital-free days alive at day 28 and higher in-hospital mortality.

CONCLUSION: In ICU patients without ARDS, ventilation with lower tidal volumes (at or below 7 ml/kg PBW) is associated with a lower risk of developing pulmonary complications, supporting a lung-protective strategy even before ARDS is present. The authors note that most earlier meta-analysis data came from intraoperative ventilation during general anaesthesia, and this analysis specifically addresses the ICU population.
title: Lung-protective ventilation with lower tidal volumes in ICU patients without ARDS (IPD meta-analysis)
